results.Notes: PASS. The shelf-audit setting is plausible and the answer turns on a legally meaningful product/package distinction rather than ingredient recall. The distractors reflect genuine confusions about ingredient-wide OTC status, insurance processing, and broad naloxone access. Full-bank comparison found MA-Q-0097 uses the same general naloxone area but tests a different decision path—third-party recipient/standing-order access—whereas MA-Q-0098 tests OTC-versus-prescription product classification and inventory/retail handling.

FAIL on strict full-bank distinctness. Although the palliative-care facts are plausible and legally correct, MA-Q-0110 is a near-duplicate decision path of released MA-Q-0111. Both are community-pharmacy technician/pharmacist scenarios that require the same sequence: identify a Schedule II/III dispensing, recognize one of the enumerated M.G.L. c.94C §21 pamphlet exceptions, and conclude that the pamphlet is not required. Several distractor roles also overlap (no-exception claim, prescriber-waiver claim, and misstatement of the exception's scope). Changing the drug from buprenorphine-naloxone to morphine and changing the enumerated exception from OUD treatment to outpatient palliative care does not create a sufficiently distinct pharmacist decision path under Issue #31's strict near-duplicate standard. A material redesign would be required; no canonical repair is performed in this audit.
